design.question: Does {program} refuse an ECDSA P-256 signature when one of its two numbers (r or s) is zero or outside the allowed range?
design.why: Why it matters: a program that does not refuse such numbers may accept a signature that the key's owner never made, and the published note for these cases says such a signature can be forged without even knowing the message, so changed data could pass as properly signed.

parsed.expect: I expect the affected version to accept at least one of these must-reject signatures, most likely one where r and s are each zero or equal to the limit n (such as case 168, r=0 and s=0) and possibly one where a valid r is left unreduced above n (such as case 477), because it calculates with r and s without first refusing values outside 1 to n-1, and these cases point to that missing check and not to another fault because each is a plain pair of whole numbers with no encoding or type fault flagged in the file and with r or s at or beyond an edge of that range, which is why the wrong-type and damaged-encoding kinds are left out.

The one building block: "signature_cases" (Published signature cases)
- What it does: Hands the program published ECDSA P-256 signatures (Project Wycheproof, pinned by SHA-256), one at a time, and compares its accept or reject with the published right answer.
- What it fits: A program or library that checks ECDSA P-256 signatures over SHA-256, in DER form.
- Its control: "accept_all_verifier". A deliberately broken checker that accepts every signature. It must get every must-reject case wrong, so the selection needs at least one must-reject case.
- Its pass rule: Passed only if every answer is right. Any wrong answer means Failed.
- It cannot test: timing or other side channels; signing (only checking); any other curve, hash or signature scheme; a crash that the program turns into a plain rejection.

The published cases it can run come from Project Wycheproof, file ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256_test.json (484 cases). The file groups its cases by kind (a "flag"). For each kind: how many cases, how many must be rejected or accepted, and the file's own published note.

quote.text: A flaw was found in all python-ecdsa versions before 0.13.3

parsed.notes: The project's own 0.13.3 release notes, as excerpted in S2, do not name CVE-2019-14859: they describe the fix under the number CVE-2019-14853, covering both a denial of service (DoS) from decoding malformed signatures and signature malleability. The advisory record (S1) describes only the acceptance of malformed signatures. What the sources describe is a signature whose bytes break the DER rules being accepted; they do not show a signature for a different message, or one made without the key, being accepted. The flaw is in reading signatures in DER form: the 0.13.2 DER reader (S4) lacks the shortest-form checks, and several of the length checks, that 0.13.3 has (S3). The signature decoder (S5) is given for 0.13.3 only, so the sources do not show whether its refusal of extra bytes after the signature is new.
parsed.weakness: When python-ecdsa before 0.13.3 reads a signature written in DER form (a strict byte layout), it does not check that the bytes really follow the DER rules, such as writing numbers and lengths in their shortest form with no unneeded zero bytes. A signature whose bytes break those rules can still be accepted, so the same signature can be rewritten as different bytes that also pass (the advisory calls this a malleable signature).

weakness_quote.text: it did not correctly verify whether signatures used DER encoding. Without this verification, a malformed signature could be accepted, making the signature malleable.

<excerpt source="S3" number="1">
def remove_sequence(string):
    if not string:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Empty string does not encode a sequence")
    if not string.startswith(b("\x30")):
        n = string[0] if isinstance(string[0], integer_types) else \
                ord(string[0])
        raise UnexpectedDER("wanted type 'sequence' (0x30), got 0x%02x" % n)
    length, lengthlength = read_length(string[1:])
    if length > len(string) - 1 - lengthlength:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Length longer than the provided buffer")
    endseq = 1+lengthlength+length
    return string[1+lengthlength:endseq], string[endseq:]
</excerpt>

<excerpt source="S3" number="2">
def remove_integer(string):
    if not string:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Empty string is an invalid encoding of an "
                            "integer")
    if not string.startswith(b("\x02")):
        n = string[0] if isinstance(string[0], integer_types) \
                else ord(string[0])
        raise UnexpectedDER("wanted type 'integer' (0x02), got 0x%02x" % n)
    length, llen = read_length(string[1:])
    if length > len(string) - 1 - llen:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Length longer than provided buffer")
    if length == 0:
        raise UnexpectedDER("0-byte long encoding of integer")
    numberbytes = string[1+llen:1+llen+length]
    rest = string[1+llen+length:]
    msb = numberbytes[0] if isinstance(numberbytes[0], integer_types) \
            else ord(numberbytes[0])
    if not msb < 0x80:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Negative integers are not supported")
    # check if the encoding is the minimal one (DER requirement)
    if length > 1 and not msb:
        # leading zero byte is allowed if the integer would have been
        # considered a negative number otherwise
        smsb = numberbytes[1] if isinstance(numberbytes[1], integer_types) \
                else ord(numberbytes[1])
        if smsb < 0x80:
            raise UnexpectedDER("Invalid encoding of integer, unnecessary "
                                "zero padding bytes")
    return int(binascii.hexlify(numberbytes), 16), rest
</excerpt>

<excerpt source="S3" number="3">
def read_length(string):
    if not string:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Empty string can't encode valid length value")
    num = string[0] if isinstance(string[0], integer_types) else ord(string[0])
    if not (num & 0x80):
        # short form
        return (num & 0x7f), 1
    # else long-form: b0&0x7f is number of additional base256 length bytes,
    # big-endian
    llen = num & 0x7f
    if not llen:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Invalid length encoding, length of length is 0")
    if llen > len(string)-1:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Length of length longer than provided buffer")
    # verify that the encoding is minimal possible (DER requirement)
    msb = string[1] if isinstance(string[1], integer_types) else ord(string[1])
    if not msb or llen == 1 and msb < 0x80:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Not minimal encoding of length")
    return int(binascii.hexlify(string[1:1+llen]), 16), 1+llen
</excerpt>

<excerpt source="S5" number="1">
def sigdecode_der(sig_der, order):
    #return der.encode_sequence(der.encode_integer(r), der.encode_integer(s))
    rs_strings, empty = der.remove_sequence(sig_der)
    if empty != b(""):
        raise der.UnexpectedDER("trailing junk after DER sig: %s" %
                                binascii.hexlify(empty))
    r, rest = der.remove_integer(rs_strings)
    s, empty = der.remove_integer(rest)
    if empty != b(""):
        raise der.UnexpectedDER("trailing junk after DER numbers: %s" %
                                binascii.hexlify(empty))
    return r, s
</excerpt>

class TestRemoveInteger(unittest.TestCase):
    # DER requires the integers to be 0-padded only if they would be
    # interpreted as negative, check if those errors are detected
    def test_non_minimal_encoding(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            remove_integer(b('\x02\x02\x00\x01'))

    def test_negative_with_high_bit_set(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            remove_integer(b('\x02\x01\x80'))

    def test_two_zero_bytes_with_high_bit_set(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            remove_integer(b('\x02\x03\x00\x00\xff'))

    def test_zero_length_integer(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            remove_integer(b('\x02\x00'))

    def test_empty_string(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            remove_integer(b(''))

    def test_encoding_of_zero(self):
        val, rem = remove_integer(b('\x02\x01\x00'))

        self.assertEqual(val, 0)
        self.assertFalse(rem)

    def test_encoding_of_127(self):
        val, rem = remove_integer(b('\x02\x01\x7f'))

        self.assertEqual(val, 127)
        self.assertFalse(rem)

    def test_encoding_of_128(self):
        val, rem = remove_integer(b('\x02\x02\x00\x80'))

        self.assertEqual(val, 128)
        self.assertFalse(rem)
</excerpt>

<excerpt source="S6" number="2">
class TestReadLength(unittest.TestCase):
    # DER requires the lengths between 0 and 127 to be encoded using the short
    # form and lengths above that encoded with minimal number of bytes
    # necessary
    def test_zero_length(self):
        self.assertEqual((0, 1), read_length(b('\x00')))

    def test_two_byte_zero_length(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            read_length(b('\x81\x00'))

    def test_two_byte_small_length(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            read_length(b('\x81\x7f'))

    def test_long_form_with_zero_length(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            read_length(b('\x80'))

    def test_smallest_two_byte_length(self):
        self.assertEqual((128, 2), read_length(b('\x81\x80')))

    def test_zero_padded_length(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            read_length(b('\x82\x00\x80'))

    def test_two_three_byte_length(self):
        self.assertEqual((256, 3), read_length(b'\x82\x01\x00'))

    def test_empty_string(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            read_length(b(''))

    def test_length_overflow(self):
        with self.assertRaises(UnexpectedDER):
            read_length(b('\x83\x01\x00'))
</excerpt>

  "notes": "Anything a reader must know to avoid a wrong conclusion, or an empty string."
}

Rules:
- Every "text" in a quote must be copied character for character from one excerpt of the source you name: at most 300 characters, from a single line where you can. If you cannot quote it, do not claim it.
- "fixed" is the first version that the publisher's own material shows as holding the fix. If the sources do not show one, write null in place of the object.
- "kind" says what the affected software does: accepts a signature it must reject, rejects one it must accept, stops with an error, or something else. "area" says where: checking ECDSA signatures, checking EdDSA signatures, or something else.
- Do not rate how serious this is, do not say how likely an attack is, and do not use the words "secure", "severity", "critical" or "score" in your own sentences. Do not quote a line that only gives a rating.
- Write for an engineer who is not a cryptographer.

design.question: Does {program} refuse a signature whose numbers are valid but whose bytes break the strict DER rules, such as a length written in a longer form than needed or a number with unneeded zero bytes in front?
design.why: Why it matters: if a signature that breaks the DER rules is still accepted, the same signature can be rewritten as different bytes that also pass, which can mislead a system that relies on each signature having only one valid byte form.

parsed.expect: I expect the affected version to accept at least one of these must-reject signatures, most likely one whose length is written in long form or with a leading zero, or one with unneeded zero bytes in front of r or s, and because every chosen case keeps the valid r and s and changes only how the bytes are written (the BerEncodedSignature kind is the one whose published note names this CVE, and cases 84 and 128 add unneeded zero bytes to the numbers), a wrong accept can come only from the missing DER checks and not from the signature arithmetic, the range checks on r and s, or extra bytes after the signature.

step.prompt:
You are helping a security test lab design a test for one published weakness. The lab can only run tests built from the building blocks listed below. You choose from them; you cannot add code, commands or new cases. If no building block can show this weakness, say so: an honest "no test" is a good answer, and a test that cannot catch the weakness is a bad one.

Advisory: CVE-2019-14859 (other names: GHSA-8qxj-f9rh-9fg2)
Package: python-ecdsa (PyPI)
Published: 2020-04-01

The lab's reading of the advisory (already checked against the publisher's text):

{
  "affected": {
    "quote": {
      "source": "S1",
      "text": "A flaw was found in all python-ecdsa versions before 0.13.3"
    },
    "versions": "all python-ecdsa versions before 0.13.3"
  },
  "area": "ecdsa_signature_check",
  "fixed": {
    "quote": {
      "source": "S1",
      "text": "\"fixed\": \"0.13.3\""
    },
    "version": "0.13.3"
  },
  "kind": "accepts_bad_signature",
  "notes": "The project's own 0.13.3 release notes, as excerpted in S2, do not name CVE-2019-14859: they describe the fix under the number CVE-2019-14853, covering both a denial of service (DoS) from decoding malformed signatures and signature malleability. The advisory record (S1) describes only the acceptance of malformed signatures. What the sources describe is a signature whose bytes break the DER rules being accepted; they do not show a signature for a different message, or one made without the key, being accepted. The flaw is in reading signatures in DER form: the 0.13.2 DER reader (S4) lacks the shortest-form checks, and several of the length checks, that 0.13.3 has (S3). The signature decoder (S5) is given for 0.13.3 only, so the sources do not show whether its refusal of extra bytes after the signature is new.",
  "plain_name": "Badly encoded signature accepted",
  "weakness": "When python-ecdsa before 0.13.3 reads a signature written in DER form (a strict byte layout), it does not check that the bytes really follow the DER rules, such as writing numbers and lengths in their shortest form with no unneeded zero bytes. A signature whose bytes break those rules can still be accepted, so the same signature can be rewritten as different bytes that also pass (the advisory calls this a malleable signature).",
  "weakness_quote": {
    "source": "S1",
    "text": "it did not correctly verify whether signatures used DER encoding. Without this verification, a malformed signature could be accepted, making the signature malleable."
  }
}

The one building block: "signature_cases" (Published signature cases)
- What it does: Hands the program published ECDSA P-256 signatures (Project Wycheproof, pinned by SHA-256), one at a time, and compares its accept or reject with the published right answer.
- What it fits: A program or library that checks ECDSA P-256 signatures over SHA-256, in DER form.
- Its control: "accept_all_verifier". A deliberately broken checker that accepts every signature. It must get every must-reject case wrong, so the selection needs at least one must-reject case.
- Its pass rule: Passed only if every answer is right. Any wrong answer means Failed.
- It cannot test: timing or other side channels; signing (only checking); any other curve, hash or signature scheme; a crash that the program turns into a plain rejection.

The published cases it can run come from Project Wycheproof, file ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256_test.json (484 cases). The file groups its cases by kind (a "flag"). For each kind: how many cases, how many must be rejected or accepted, and the file's own published note.

<excerpt source="S1" number="2">
## possible DoS in signature verification and signature malleability 

### Impact
Code using `VerifyingKey.verify()` and `VerifyingKey.verify_digest()` may receive exceptions other than the documented `BadSignatureError` when signatures are malformed. If those other exceptions are not caught, they may lead to program termination and thus Denial of Service

Code using `VerifyingKey.verify()` and `VerifyingKey.verify_digest()` with `sigdecode` option using `ecdsa.util.sigdecode_der` will accept signatures even if they are not properly formatted DER. This makes the signatures malleable. It impacts only applications that later sign the signatures or verify signatures of signatures, e.g. Bitcoin.

All versions between 0.5 and 0.13.2 (inclusive) are thought to be vulnerable. Code before 0.5 may be vulnerable but didn't receive extended analysis to rule this issue out.

### Patches
The patches have been merged to `master` branch in https://github.com/warner/python-ecdsa/pull/115.
The backported patches for a release in the 0.13 branch are in https://github.com/warner/python-ecdsa/pull/124

They are part of the 0.13.3 release.

There are no plans to backport them to earlier releases.

### Workarounds
It may be possible to prevent the Denial of Service by catching also `UnexpectedDER`, `IndexError` and `AssertionError` exceptions. That list hasn't been verified to be complete though. If those exceptions are raised, the signature verification process should consider the signature to be invalid.

To remediate signature malleability and the Denial of Service vulnerability, it may be possible to first verify that the signature is properly DER formatted ECDSA-Sig-Value, as defined in [RFC3279](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3279), before passing it to `verify()` or `verify_digest()` methods. If the signature is determined to not follow the DER or encode a different structure, the signature verification process should consider the signature to be invalid.

### References
https://en.bitcoinwiki.org/wiki/Transaction_Malleability

### For more information
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory please open an issue in [python-ecdsa](https://github.com/warner/python-ecdsa/issues) project.

</excerpt>

def remove_integer(string):
    if not string:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Empty string is an invalid encoding of an "
                            "integer")
    if not string.startswith(b("\x02")):
        n = string[0] if isinstance(string[0], integer_types) \
                else ord(string[0])
        raise UnexpectedDER("wanted type 'integer' (0x02), got 0x%02x" % n)
    length, llen = read_length(string[1:])
    if length > len(string) - 1 - llen:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Length longer than provided buffer")
    if length == 0:
        raise UnexpectedDER("0-byte long encoding of integer")
    numberbytes = string[1+llen:1+llen+length]
    rest = string[1+llen+length:]
    msb = numberbytes[0] if isinstance(numberbytes[0], integer_types) \
            else ord(numberbytes[0])
    if not msb < 0x80:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Negative integers are not supported")
    # check if the encoding is the minimal one (DER requirement)
    if length > 1 and not msb:
        # leading zero byte is allowed if the integer would have been
        # considered a negative number otherwise
        smsb = numberbytes[1] if isinstance(numberbytes[1], integer_types) \
                else ord(numberbytes[1])
        if smsb < 0x80:
            raise UnexpectedDER("Invalid encoding of integer, unnecessary "
                                "zero padding bytes")
    return int(binascii.hexlify(numberbytes), 16), rest

  "question": "Does {program} refuse a signature whose two numbers are right but whose bytes break the strict DER format, such as a length written in a longer form than needed or a number padded with extra zero bytes?",
  "why": "Why it matters: if a checker accepts several byte forms of one signature, anyone can rewrite a valid signature into a different-looking one that still passes, which the advisory says affects only applications that later sign the signatures or check signatures of signatures, such as Bitcoin.",
  "select": {"flags": ["BerEncodedSignature"], "ids": ["84", "128"]},
  "control": "accept_all_verifier",
  "expect": "The affected version is expected to wrongly accept some of these must-reject signatures, most directly the numbers padded with unneeded zero bytes (ids 84 and 128), which the sources show 0.13.3 refuses and 0.13.2 does not check, and probably the over-long and indefinite length forms as well; each chosen case keeps the valid r and s and changes only the byte format, so a wrong accept points to the advisory's loose DER reading and not to a fault in range checks or arithmetic, and the advisory's other half, the wrong error type on a malformed signature, is not shown because this block cannot see an error that the program turns into a plain rejection."
}

step.prompt:
You are helping a security test lab design a test for one published weakness. The lab can only run tests built from the building blocks listed below. You choose from them; you cannot add code, commands or new cases. If no building block can show this weakness, say so: an honest "no test" is a good answer, and a test that cannot catch the weakness is a bad one.

Advisory: CVE-2019-14853 (other names: GHSA-pwfw-mgfj-7g3g)
Package: python-ecdsa (PyPI)
Published: 2019-10-08

The lab's reading of the advisory (already checked against the publisher's text):

{
  "affected": {
    "quote": {
      "source": "S1",
      "text": "All versions between 0.5 and 0.13.2 (inclusive) are thought to be vulnerable. Code before 0.5 may be vulnerable but didn't receive extended analysis to rule this issue out."
    },
    "versions": "All versions between 0.5 and 0.13.2 (inclusive) are thought to be vulnerable; versions before 0.5 may be vulnerable but did not receive extended analysis. The record's range data starts at version 0, so it counts every version before 0.13.3."
  },
  "area": "ecdsa_signature_check",
  "fixed": {
    "quote": {
      "source": "S1",
      "text": "They are part of the 0.13.3 release."
    },
    "version": "0.13.3"
  },
  "kind": "stops_with_error",
  "notes": "The advisory covers two separate problems, and the kind above records only the first. (1) Wrong error type: this library reports a rejected signature by raising BadSignatureError (it returns True when the signature passes), so an error on a bad signature is not the fault by itself. The fault is a different error type raised for a malformed signature, and the program stops only if the calling code does not catch it. As other error types to catch, the advisory names UnexpectedDER, IndexError and AssertionError, and says that list has not been verified to be complete. This is not limited to DER signatures: for the default fixed-length format, 0.13.2 checks the length with an assert (S8) and 0.13.3 turns that case into BadSignatureError (S7, S3). (2) Loose DER reading, which the advisory calls signature malleability: with ecdsa.util.sigdecode_der, signatures that are not properly formatted DER are accepted. For example, 0.13.3 refuses a number padded with unnecessary zero bytes (S5) and the 0.13.2 code shown has no such check (S6). The advisory says this affects only applications that later sign the signatures or verify signatures of signatures, such as Bitcoin; the sources do not say that a signature for different data or from a different key is accepted. The advisory says there are no plans to backport the fix to earlier releases, and the 0.13.3 release notes (S2) name this CVE as fixed in that release.",
  "plain_name": "Malformed signature raises unexpected error",
  "weakness": "When given a malformed signature, VerifyingKey.verify() and verify_digest() can raise errors other than the documented BadSignatureError, and a program that does not catch them may stop. With the DER decoder (sigdecode_der) they also accept signatures that do not properly follow the DER byte format.",
  "weakness_quote": {
    "source": "S1",
    "text": "Code using `VerifyingKey.verify()` and `VerifyingKey.verify_digest()` may receive exceptions other than the documented `BadSignatureError` when signatures are malformed. If those other exceptions are not caught, they may lead to program termination and thus Denial of Service"
  }
}

The one building block: "signature_cases" (Published signature cases)
- What it does: Hands the program published ECDSA P-256 signatures (Project Wycheproof, pinned by SHA-256), one at a time, and compares its accept or reject with the published right answer.
- What it fits: A program or library that checks ECDSA P-256 signatures over SHA-256, in DER form.
- Its control: "accept_all_verifier". A deliberately broken checker that accepts every signature. It must get every must-reject case wrong, so the selection needs at least one must-reject case.
- Its pass rule: Passed only if every answer is right. Any wrong answer means Failed.
- It cannot test: timing or other side channels; signing (only checking); any other curve, hash or signature scheme; a crash that the program turns into a plain rejection.

The published cases it can run come from Project Wycheproof, file ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256_test.json (484 cases). The file groups its cases by kind (a "flag"). For each kind: how many cases, how many must be rejected or accepted, and the file's own published note.

def read_length(string):
    if not string:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Empty string can't encode valid length value")
    num = string[0] if isinstance(string[0], integer_types) else ord(string[0])
    if not (num & 0x80):
        # short form
        return (num & 0x7f), 1
    # else long-form: b0&0x7f is number of additional base256 length bytes,
    # big-endian
    llen = num & 0x7f
    if not llen:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Invalid length encoding, length of length is 0")
    if llen > len(string)-1:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Length of length longer than provided buffer")
    # verify that the encoding is minimal possible (DER requirement)
    msb = string[1] if isinstance(string[1], integer_types) else ord(string[1])
    if not msb or llen == 1 and msb < 0x80:
        raise UnexpectedDER("Not minimal encoding of length")
    return int(binascii.hexlify(string[1:1+llen]), 16), 1+llen

The one building block: "signature_cases" (Published signature cases)
- What it does: Hands the program published ECDSA P-256 signatures (Project Wycheproof, pinned by SHA-256), one at a time, and compares its accept or reject with the published right answer.
- What it fits: A program or library that checks ECDSA P-256 signatures over SHA-256, in DER form.
- Its control: "accept_all_verifier". A deliberately broken checker that accepts every signature. It must get every must-reject case wrong, so the selection needs at least one must-reject case.
- Its pass rule: Passed only if every answer is right. Any wrong answer means Failed.
- It cannot test: timing or other side channels; signing (only checking); any other curve, hash or signature scheme; a crash that the program turns into a plain rejection.

The published cases it can run come from Project Wycheproof, file ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256_test.json (484 cases). The file groups its cases by kind (a "flag"). For each kind: how many cases, how many must be rejected or accepted, and the file's own published note.

The one building block: "signature_cases" (Published signature cases)
- What it does: Hands the program published ECDSA P-256 signatures (Project Wycheproof, pinned by SHA-256), one at a time, and compares its accept or reject with the published right answer.
- What it fits: A program or library that checks ECDSA P-256 signatures over SHA-256, in DER form.
- Its control: "accept_all_verifier". A deliberately broken checker that accepts every signature. It must get every must-reject case wrong, so the selection needs at least one must-reject case.
- Its pass rule: Passed only if every answer is right. Any wrong answer means Failed.
- It cannot test: timing or other side channels; signing (only checking); any other curve, hash or signature scheme; a crash that the program turns into a plain rejection.

The published cases it can run come from Project Wycheproof, file ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256_test.json (484 cases). The file groups its cases by kind (a "flag"). For each kind: how many cases, how many must be rejected or accepted, and the file's own published note.

The one building block: "signature_cases" (Published signature cases)
- What it does: Hands the program published ECDSA P-256 signatures (Project Wycheproof, pinned by SHA-256), one at a time, and compares its accept or reject with the published right answer.
- What it fits: A program or library that checks ECDSA P-256 signatures over SHA-256, in DER form.
- Its control: "accept_all_verifier". A deliberately broken checker that accepts every signature. It must get every must-reject case wrong, so the selection needs at least one must-reject case.
- Its pass rule: Passed only if every answer is right. Any wrong answer means Failed.
- It cannot test: timing or other side channels; signing (only checking); any other curve, hash or signature scheme; a crash that the program turns into a plain rejection.

The published cases it can run come from Project Wycheproof, file ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256_test.json (484 cases). The file groups its cases by kind (a "flag"). For each kind: how many cases, how many must be rejected or accepted, and the file's own published note.
